title: Structural Characterization of Brain-Derived Tau Fibrils From Alzheimer’s Disease Patient Tissue
content: Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disease that is characterized by cognitive decline, motor impairment, dementia, and death. AD is the most prevalent neurodegenerative disease affecting ∼10% of individuals over the age of 65 [1]. A hallmark of this diagnosis is aggregation and fibrilization of small soluble neuronal proteins—among them tau [2]. Tau is an intrinsically disordered protein that binds to and promotes the assembly and stability of microtubules in neurons [3]. Six isoforms are present in humans and are regulated by alternative splicing. However, through post translational modifications, familial mutations, and aging, tau can aggregate into fibrils. Fibril growth responsible for neurodegeneration occurs by primary nucleation events in which monomeric protein factors come together to form highly stable β-sheets that stack along the fibril axis. These fibrils interact with cellular organelles and other tau fibrils and develop into neurofibrillary tangles that can impair microtubule function, interrupt cellular processes, and lead to neuronal toxicity [4].
